stories.body:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.

A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.

Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.

The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.

“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.

The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.

Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.

A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.

Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.

The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong.

The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

stories.title: Trump declares robot imports a national security threat
stories.summary: President orders trade talks on foreign-made factory robots, threatens tariffs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
President orders trade talks on foreign-made factory robots, threatens tariffs.

President Donald Trump has declared the imports of foreign-made factory robots to be a national security threat—ordering new US negotiations with trading partners while holding out the possibility of imposing new tariffs on such robot imports in the future.

Issued on October 28, Trump’s presidential proclamation represents heightened government scrutiny of foreign-made industrial robots that could complicate the manufacturing operations of major US corporations that rely on such robots. Those companies include Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford, electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla , and aerospace and defense giants like Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Trump’s proclamation describes industrial robots and machinery as being crucial for producing US military weapon systems along with representing a “driving force” behind all critical infrastructure sectors within the US economy. The proclamation cites an investigation under US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick as having found that US imports of such robots “pose[] risks to the United States industrial base and threatens the long-term competitiveness of the United States in a sector that is increasingly vital to national security.”

The Department of Commerce investigation also supposedly found “unique security and safety risks” that may introduce “significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities that can result in severe consequences to the United States.”

Such wording echoes justifications used by Trump’s Federal Communications Commission when it banned new models of foreign-made robots, such as robotic vacuums, four-legged robot dogs, and humanoid robots, in July 2026. But that FCC action had specifically exempted industrial robot arms and other fixed or stationary robots commonly deployed in automotive factories and logistics warehouses.

Now Trump’s directive for the United States and trading partners “to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components” aims to strike new agreements on the issue within 180 days of the proclamation’s date. If no agreements have been reached by then, the proclamation warns that the president may take additional actions, like imposing “tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees” on such imports.

Any tariffs or other fees would, of course, be paid by the US companies importing such foreign-made robots. That would likely increase the cost of US manufacturing operations at a time when the United States has become the second largest market in using industrial robots, with the International Federation of Robotics reporting nearly 38,500 new US installations of industrial robots in 2025.

Major US automotive and aerospace companies often buy large robotic arms for factory floor work from the “big four” robotics makers—FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa, and KUKA—that are headquartered in Japan, Switzerland, and Germany. No US company currently offers comparable heavy-duty hardware for large industrial robotic arms, although the foreign robotics makers have been expanding their US engineering and assembly facilities.

Even Amazon, the company that has arguably deployed more robot workers than any other in the world, still uses some foreign-made robots, like Japan’s FANUC robotic arms, despite having significantly ramped up its own in-house robot production and developed certain specialized robotic arms.

Trump’s own proclamation acknowledges that US robotics companies do not produce enough industrial robots to “meet national security needs,” and that the United States “relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery and for their components.”

If Trump eventually slaps tariffs on US imports of foreign-made industrial robots, that would at least fall short of restricting imports outright. Although as Intel recently showed, major US companies can still get waivers from the Trump administration to continue using foreign-made robots even when a nominal ban is in place.

stories.body:
Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loom

The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.

Estimates ranged from ⁠a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.

The growth comes as resilient consumer spending and AI -driven ⁠business investment has more than ⁠offset the impact ​of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East .

The change is in stark contrast to ​households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in ‌ Donald Trump ’s record-low approval ratings ‌and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of about 2%. New data from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, showed that prices increased 0.5% for the month in September and the annualized inflation rate rose to 3.6%. In August, the PCE’s inflation rate was 3.4%.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to an annualized 3.1%.

The consumer price index , a separate measure of inflation released by the Department of Labor that was released earlier in October, had also shown inflation rising in September, with the annualized inflation rate going from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September.

Despite the rise in prices, the US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.

Increasing interest rates can slow inflation, at the risk of slackening economic activity and the jobs market. Because inflation is still hot, economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding ‌at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”

Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the ​strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect ⁠this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.

Consumer spending, ​which accounts for more ​than two-thirds of the economy, increased at ​a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in ​the second quarter. Historically low ‌layoffs and moderate ​hiring are helping ​to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged behind inflation.

But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon – about $1 a gallon more than a year ago – as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipate a slowdown in consumer spending.

Multiple polls have shown Donald Trump’s approval rating on the economy have plummeted in the weeks before the election, with voters citing frustration over rising gas and grocery prices. Overall consumer sentiment , measured by the University of Michigan is down 15% from February, before the start of the war with Iran, as consumers expect more inflation to come.

stories.title: DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
stories.summary: The DUP leader Gavin Robinson also confirms that Emma Little-Pengelly will not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Michelle O'Neill described the move as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented"

Published 29 October 2026

Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has been blocked by the DUP from attending an economic summit involving Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The Sinn Féin vice-president and Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly were both invited to attend the National Economic Council in Glasgow on Friday with other devolved leaders.

The DUP leader Gavin Robinson confirmed that his party colleague Little-Pengelly will not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill and permission will not be granted for the first minister to operate on a solo basis.

The move follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests which prevented a contentious Orange Order march in Portadown from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road .

Robinson was flanked by DUP assembly members as he spoke in the Great Hall at Parliament Buildings

A meeting of the party's ruling officer committee was held earlier on Thursday.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the first minister's "arrogance will have consequences", but O'Neill accused the party of being "reckless and irresponsible".

"Her complaints today that she's frustrated from engaging with the British Prime Minister within the sovereign United Kingdom will so be it because her law breaking must have consequences," Robinson said.

O'Neill said the DUP leader's comments were "arrogant and supremacist" adding that the DUP "is consumed with their own internal leadership troubles and divisions".

She said she would be at the Assembly on Monday with her party colleagues to "keep showing up every day for people".

Earlier she described the move to block the meeting with the prime minister as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented".

"This is a reactive stunt, driven by the DUP's own internal pressures and electoral problems," she said in a statement posted online.

The prime minister revived the National Economic Council over the summer to encourage greater collaboration between the nations and regions.

Earlier Little-Pengelly said the concerns arising from O'Neill's conduct and the "anger and hurt felt by many people across Northern Ireland, cannot simply be ignored or minimised".

She said the decision comes after stopping a separate planned engagement with the President of Ireland, Catherine Connolly.

"I have requested a separate meeting with the Prime Minister to ensure Northern Ireland's interests, including the urgent budgetary and funding challenges facing the Executive, continue to be represented directly," she added.

The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it was "deeply frustrating" that the Northern Ireland executive would not be represented at the National Economic Council.

"I understand feelings are running high but it must be in the interests of the people of Northern Ireland that everyone gets round the table."

The DUP ruling committee met to discuss what steps it would take against Sinn Féin over the Drumcree dispute

O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating last month's unnotified demonstrations in Portadown , with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

The Sinn Féin deputy leader has defended her involvement, saying it was the "right thing to do".

The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said "the DUP's sham response today was beyond pathetic" adding "the DUP is interested only in clinging to office, not principle".

Alliance leader Naomi Long said refusing to attend or preventing others from attending the meeting with the prime minister was reckless and put party interests ahead of Northern Ireland's economic future and the needs of the public.

The Ulster Unionist Party leader Jon Burrows told BBC's Evening Extra programme the situation was a "political fudge" that was "all choreography and no consequences," adding that the move would "probably galvanise Sinn Féin further at the ballot box."

The Social Democratic and Labour Party's (SDLP) Matthew O'Toole said "plunging this place into more political chaos is not a sensible strategic move for unionism".

"Ultimately it's only going to make reasonable people here conclude that the largest unionist party simply doesn't want to make the status quo work," he added.

The DUP has been under pressure from unionist rivals and some within its own ranks over how to respond to the row over Drumcree.

Last week, DUP MP Carla Lockhart stepped down from the party's officer board over their leader Gavin Robinson not withdrawing Little-Pengelly to force O'Neill from their joint Stormont office.

On Thursday Lockhart said she will follow her "own course" if the party does not seek to remove Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill as Stormont's first minister.

Robinson said that while O'Neill and her party colleagues "should be punished, that does not include punishing the rest of Northern Ireland".

The Upper Bann MP, who last week quit the DUP's ruling officer board in opposition to party leader Gavin Robinson's approach, outlined her position in a letter to colleagues which she later posted on Facebook.

Other DUP representatives including assembly member Diane Forsythe have since backed Lockhart's calls for O'Neill to be "removed from office" .

On Tuesday, Forsythe said that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".

On Wednesday, a second DUP assembly member called for O'Neill to go.

Maurice Bradley said removing O'Neill "would not, in itself, require the Assembly to collapse".

Carla Lockhart stepped down from the DUP's officer board last week

Bradley added that the party "must stand together" and "support Carla Lockhart".

Other party members including former MP Lord McCrea and Mid Ulster councillor Clement Cuthbertson have also backed Lockhart.

Party leader Robinson said last week that he was "sorry" to see Lockhart quit the DUP's officer board but added that she remained "a key part of our team".

Speaking on the BBC's The View programme , Robinson said the party had reached a democratic decision on how to deal with the Drumcree fallout.

He questioned whether it was necessary to "punish everyone in Northern Ireland when actually we should be punishing those who broke the law".

"We have considered all options and we keep all options on the table," he added.

Last week, a court heard Police Service of Northern Ireland intelligence information that dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on police had officers cleared a path for the parade.

stories.title: MP apologises over bullying and harassment
stories.summary: Tony Vaughan is found to have been "overbearing and belittling" towards a female staff member.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tony Vaughan (pictured) has shown remorse, according to a report

Published 29 October 2026

A Labour MP has said sorry in the House of Commons following complaints over his behaviour towards a female member of staff.

It comes as the Independent Expert Panel published a report , external requiring Tony Vaughan to apologise for breaching Parliament's bullying and harassment policy.

The MP for Folkestone and Hythe was found by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards to have committed the breach after a constituency staff member complained he "behaved towards [her] in an overbearing and belittling manner".

Vaughan said on Thursday he accepted the findings in full.

"As a result of these behaviours, my former colleague was upset and humiliated," he said.

"My behaviour had a real and continuing impact on her and her family, and I am truly sorry for this."

The Labour Party said it "expects the highest standards of conduct from all our members and elected representatives.

"We have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld.

"It is right that Tony Vaughan has apologised following this independent process," a spokesperson added.

'Abuse of power'

Vaughan, who has represented his Kent constituency since 2024, was found to have hugged the complainant without consent at an office event.

He also took her personal mobile phone from her hand to join an online meeting without asking permission and failed to explain why phone calls between them had ended abruptly.

Vaughan appealed the Commissioner's findings, though the Independent Expert Panel confirmed the majority of them, according to Parliament.

The sub-panel stressed that "oppressive and bullying behaviour towards [MPs'] staff members is wholly unacceptable".

It added that Vaughan's actions were breaches of "basic boundaries and courtesy" - rather than failures in management - and an "abuse of his power".

Watch: MP apologises over bullying and harassment

The politician told MPs on Thursday that he was not "sufficiently alert" to the power imbalances between him and his employee.

He added he recognised his behaviour could well impact on "someone who is vulnerable whether or not that is known".

"I made mistakes," Vaughan continued.

The 36-page report said it took account of the impact of what happened on the complainant, who has a right to anonymity.

She said she was left feeling stressed, exhausted and offended, it adds.

The report also stated that Vaughan had "expressed genuine and thoughtful remorse".

He should be required to make an "unreserved apology" to the complainant and the House by way of a personal statement in the House of Commons Chamber, it continued.

"We consider that this achieves the appropriate balance and clear messaging required regarding the behaviour expected of MPs," the report said.

Vaughan added he had undertaken further training as a result of the incident.

stories.title: Trump ignored intel on China’s Nvidia spy to protect company’s stock, report says
stories.summary: Spy accused of exploiting Trump ties to Huang, funneling secrets to China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Spy accused of exploiting Trump ties to Huang, funneling secrets to China.

Donald Trump apparently is so aligned with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—who has become the president’s key advisor on AI —that he ignored intelligence indicating that Huang was the target of a “Chinese spy plot,” and did so partly to protect Nvidia’s stock.

The New York Times spoke with people briefed on US intelligence agencies’ surveillance and granted them anonymity to discuss findings drawn from “classified intelligence.” According to sources, about a year ago, Trump was briefed that “Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access” to Huang. That “someone” was Alice Huang, or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and former top executive at a Singapore cloud company called Megaspeed.

According to sources, the US had already suspected that Alice Huang—who is not related to Jensen Huang—was helping China evade export controls to gain access to high-end Nvidia chips through Megaspeed. But it alarmed investigators to discover that she may have used her role at Megaspeed to gain direct access to Jensen Huang. It’s now believed she may have leveraged that closeness to feed China intel not only on one of America’s leading AI companies, but also to influence Trump’s thinking on AI. As Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted last month ahead of Trump’s AI talks with China President Xi Jinping, “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.”

At least partly due to fears that US action against the alleged spying could hobble Nvidia chip sales or disrupt the delicate US-China trade truce, Trump “chose not to do anything with the information,” sources said.

Soon after US scrutiny increased, Alice Huang’s name was removed from Megaspeed corporate documents. At this stage, it’s unclear “how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed,” NYT reported.

Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC, told NYT that the US accusations against Alice Huang are baseless. He accused the US of pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China.

No warning to Nvidia CEO

It’s not clear which agencies were investigating Alice Huang or what triggered their suspicions, NYT reported. Sources also could not explain what information she may have shared with Beijing.

Nvidia has denied that she would have had access to any trade secrets, but it seems notable that Jensen Huang did not receive a defensive briefing that Americans sometimes get when they’re targets of foreign spying. Some senior officials think it’s unlikely that Jensen Huang would have “remained unaware” of Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence-gathering for the entire duration of their professional relationship, although Trump was told Jensen Huang had no knowledge at the time of his briefing. It seems possible that Jensen Huang got no briefing because US agencies worried that he might tip her off that “she was being watched,” the NYT reported.

Trump’s deep ties with tech leaders have been criticized throughout his administration, but Jensen Huang’s influence increasingly stands out . To critics, the political friendship appears to be largely based on growing his business in China. Since cozying up to Trump, the Nvidia CEO has gotten export controls relaxed and even struck a controversial deal giving the US a 25 percent cut of some chip sales so he could try to sell more chips in China. Sources told NYT that “some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia” have “ground to a halt within the Commerce Department” due to Jensen Huang’s influence.

No one’s sure when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, but NYT found social media photos that predated her role arranging a Megaspeed purchase of $2 billion in chips over the next year. If those chips ended up in China, the US worried they “could help adversaries like China develop new weapons, surveil dissidents, and leap ahead of the United States in AI development,” NYT reported. To US agencies, it’s particularly concerning that Megaspeed may be doing China’s bidding by supplying chips to giant data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia “that appear to remotely serve customers in China,” NYT reported earlier this month.

Sources told the NYT that US intelligence agencies conducted electronic surveillance of Alice Huang and found that “she was in contact with an American citizen.” Since agencies could not legally surveil the American citizen without a court order, they sought to unmask the citizen by showing a “need for information.”

“In this case, the unmasking process identified Mr. Huang as the US citizen,” NYT reported.

NYT probes Megaspeed offices for clues

Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer, and Nvidia has independently investigated whether Megaspeed is funneling its chips to China. That investigation concluded that there were no signs of diversion and that Megaspeed has raised no red flags as a customer, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told NYT.

Both Nvidia and Megaspeed insist that the cloud company has Singapore-based owners, but NYT visited the supposed offices and talked to anyone they could find to probe the actual business operations. Among red flags raised, NYT noted that staffers suggested “it’s not clear” what Megaspeed as a company does and confirmed that the Singapore director, James Tan, lives in China and is “never present.” (NYT’s review of corporate ownership documents showed Tan owns the shell company that owns Megaspeed.)

In that story published earlier this month, NYT detailed how Alice Huang was seemingly growing increasingly close to Jensen Huang, citing several photos of them together. That includes a photo at an event where she reportedly bragged, “I bet you guys I can get Jensen here,” and then he arrived in his trademark leather jacket to take whiskey shots.

Rizzo said that it was common for Nvidia’s CEO to attend parties with customers and partners, where he discussed “updates on the market.” One source told NYT that Jensen Huang had always planned to attend that party.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” Rizzo said. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

However, the US government has been investigating Megaspeed since 2024, and they’ve found suspicious boxes of Nvidia equipment that seem to be ready to ship out, rather than installed. Earlier this year, the Department of Justice took over the Commerce Department’s investigation, and Megaspeed remains under scrutiny even though Nvidia’s probes uncovered no evidence the company was helping China dodge export curb violations.

Aaron Bartnick, an assistant director for technology security and governance under the Biden administration, told NYT that Megaspeed raised “many red flags.” Among them are the company’s “ownership claims and possible ties to sanctioned entities, that should have made Nvidia’s executives question whether they should have permitted the company to have access to its AI chips.”

“It’s hard to see a justification for taking that risk,” Bartnick said.

stories.body:
In today’s digital world, the internet is an essential resource for young people to access information, explore community, and find themselves. But we know that this often comes alongside fears of experiencing online harms like doxxing, grooming, or bullying.

Trying to protect your family from everything all the time is impractical and exhausting, but some thoughtful planning can help families devise a workable plan that meets their needs and addresses their concerns.

That’s why this Digital Parent Week, we’re sharing easy tips on how parents and their children can work together to co-curate a digital safety plan that helps all members of the family enjoy the benefits of technology while protecting their online privacy and safety.

Online safety begins with communication, not just restrictions. Talk with a young person about how they use the internet: their favourite apps, games, and social media platforms for example. Creating a supportive environment helps young people feel comfortable asking for help if something goes wrong online.

Together, you can think about:

What do we want to protect? e.g., I want to protect a young person’s privacy and mental health when they’re playing Roblox. They love Roblox and use it to communicate and hang out with their best friend, so we’d like to find a way to make it as safe as possible.

Who do we want to protect it from? e.g., messages from strangers, staying up too late playing, wasting money on pointless digital junk in games.

How bad are the consequences if we fail? e.g, losing some money on a scam or having creepy conversations with strangers that could escalate into something more nefarious or dangerous.

How likely is it that we will need to protect it? e.g., I don’t know the likelihood of a stranger messaging you on Roblox because I’m not sure how communication works on the platform, but I’ve heard from their friends that strangers message them all the time in some games.

How much trouble are we willing to go through to try to prevent potential consequences? e.g., I’m willing to learn from my child how the game works, play the game with my child, and learn how to work the parental controls.

Who are our allies? e.g., my partner, our parents, as well as a young person’s best friends and their parents.

It's easy to think of a young person's experience on the internet as being totally disconnected and different from your own. But now is a great time to also interrogate your own internet habits, like the sorts of sites you engage with, tools you use, and privacy settings you've set. These questions are as valuable to help you as a parent as they are just an internet user.

Sometimes even just figuring out what conversations are worth having can take some effort, we've put together some ideas to get you started in our guide .

Digital security training can feel overwhelming but this is why a community-oriented approach helps. In speaking with your family and friends, you can build out digital security practices that work for you. This makes it more likely that your privacy practices will become second nature to you and your loved ones.

Use secure messaging services for every communication: Choosing a secure service ensures that your privacy is protected from government and corporate surveillance. If you can convince your family to get on board, options like Signal provide the most extensive privacy protections out of the box through its use of end-to-end encryption and limited data collection. But we understand that sometimes it's easier to stick with whatever the family already uses for a group chat, like WhatsApp, Apple's iMessage, or Google Messages, so take the time to familiarize yourself with the limits of WhatsApp and RCS encryption .

Consider the content posted online: It's easy to accidentally share personal information through photos, messages, and other content. Children and adults may unknowingly share personal information through photos, messages, location settings and app permissions. Take time together to review privacy settings, check which apps can access the camera or location, and discuss why personal details should be shared carefully. Make sure you have family agreement about when and where to post photos of each other or your home.

Create incident response plans: Developing a plan for if or when something bad happens is a good practice for anyone, but especially with younger people. It’s important to strategize with your family around what to do in the event of such things happening, and doing so before an incident occurs is much easier than when you’re presently facing a crisis.

Alongside this, simple steps like using strong and unique passwords on all devices, including those that are shared in the family, can make a real difference. Regardless of age, there’s no time like the present to get started on good security hygiene, and for many that starts with a password manager and two-factor authentication .

Many sites permit parents to control features such as personalization, algorithmic feed, autoplay, endless scroll, reactions, notifications, and time limits. Talk as a family about which features are important and useful and which are problematic. The conversations above around boundaries and digital literacy are a more effective way to prepare youth for accessing the internet. To develop true autonomy, young people need the privacy to discover the world for themselves without their parents monitoring the contents of every conversation they have.

Explore new apps together and revisit family rules as they grow. These decision points where you’re exploring with a young person what you’re both comfortable with can be good moments to “find your way to a yes” for whatever feature or tool or game they’re asking about. The questions they ask, along with your responses, provide a road map for what to look for in privacy controls that can get you to a place where everyone is comfortable engaging with that technology.

There is no one size fits all to the tech questions and concerns a parent will face, and keeping young people safe online is not about removing every risk and monitoring every click. This Digital Parenting Week, you can start to focus on what’s important for your family and how to best achieve those goals.

Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China

US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.

Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.

In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.

White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.

The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.

In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.

stories.title: Victory! You Can Now Exclude Apps from Siri AI
stories.summary: In the most recent update to Apple’s devices, iOS 27.2, the company has introduced a new setting to “Exclude Apps” from Siri AI, fulfilling one of our asks from our Encrypt It Already campaign earlier this year . One of our main concerns with new AI features on devices is how those features interact with end-to-end encrypted content, particularly with secure messaging apps. Many AI features require cloud processing, and despite privacy protections engineered into these systems , the content of secure messaging apps may leave a user’s device without their knowledge. That changes the privacy concerns around using those tools. In a perfect world, users would be able to put a barrier up to ensure data from certain apps doesn’t leave the device. Here was our initial ask: You should be able to tell the operating system’s AI to not access an app, even if that comes at the “cost” of missing out on some features. The setting should be straightforward and easy to understand in ways the Gemini and Apple Intelligence controls currently are not. At launch, we found the settings to control Siri AI’s app access behavior pretty confusing . You had to toggle several options to block Siri AI off from accessing an app, or disable Siri AI entirely. Turning off Siri AI and reverting to Siri Classic is, for now, still a good option if you’d prefer to use the older version. The most recent update is far more clear and does more to protect your data. And, just as expected, it comes at the cost of some features. That’s a good thing, actually. The features not working shows that the new setting is effective. Here’s how to add apps to the exclusion list, once you’ve updated to 27.2: Open Settings > Siri > Excluded Apps Tap “Add Apps” and select any apps you’d like to add to the exclusion list Now Siri AI cannot access the contents of the app. Excluding an app also means you may lose some features. For example, if you exclude the Apple Messages app, you will no longer be able to have Siri AI read or respond to messages for you. Even the “onscreen awareness” feature, where you invoke Siri and ask it for information about what you’re currently looking at, will not work anymore. For example, if you exclude Signal, you cannot invoke Siri and ask it to discern any information in the Signal app. You’ll just get these messages: What’s the State of This on Android? Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarre mashups of popular video games . Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from. Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube for this informative video , which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more. Continue reading...

Thinktank says chancellor has given himself a mountain to climb after ducking big decisions in low-key speech

John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return to austerity, according to Britain’s leading tax and spending experts.

A day after his address to the Commons , the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking several big decisions in his debut tax and spending statement.

After his low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, the thinktank said Healey had left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms.

But as the war in the Middle East fuels a surge in inflation – raising the cost of delivering public services – the chancellor has in effect pencilled in large cuts in the run-up to the next general election.

Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

“It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review,” she said.

With Labour having promised there would be no return to austerity, and as Andy Burnham’s government prepares for the next election, she said it appeared extremely unlikely that Healey would follow through with such cuts.

“A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises,” she said.

In his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock emanating from the Middle East war.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – allowing a hit to the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drives up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

after newsletter promotion

Faced with grim forecasts for household living standards and growth in the British economy, the IFS said it was a “reasonable choice” for the chancellor to allow for a modest reduction in headroom.

However, his deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the thinktank to criticise his plans for meeting the fiscal rules, because they in effect relied on him cutting public spending or announcing tax increases that he had yet to prepare the public for.

“My concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it,” Miller said.

stories.body:
The chancellor outlined ‘the biggest wave of devolution in a generation’ – but large swathes of the country are excluded

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

In just two years, there could be dozens of mayors preparing to spend billions of pounds as part of Andy Burnham’s mission to devolve greater powers across England.

Fresh devolution deals could also be in place following negotiations with leaders in Scotland, Wales and possibly Northern Ireland, allowing the prime minister to say at the next election that he has fulfilled a promise to rewire Britain’s political landscape with a view to giving more local control.

This was the message from John Healey’s first budget , which outlined the direction of travel and put in some milestones, including a 2028 commitment to devolve some income tax receipts to mayors of strategic authorities (MSAs). He added the commitment that next year, 20% of business rates revenues will go to mayors.

He told MPs that he was offering mayors 100% of their business rates income by the end of the decade and the ability to tax visitors who stay in hotels and B&Bs in their aream, via a new overnight visitors levy.

It would mean, Healey said: “New powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics. The biggest wave of devolution in a generation, driving good growth in every postcode delivered to the British people by this Labour government.”

However, Burnham’s signature phrase that he will bring “good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” will face scrutiny once it becomes clear large parts of the country are excluded.

Manchester, the West Midlands and Liverpool City region head a list of 14 areas already governed by a mayor.

Healey said the 14 were on course to get enhanced deals, while ministers were in the final stages of signing 10 more agreements, creating MSAs for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay; Hertfordshire; Lancashire; Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland; Stoke and Staffordshire; Surrey; Thames Valley (Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Swindon); and Wessex.

Last month, Essex county council leaders agreed to adopt an MSA to secure about £1.2bn of funding over 10 years. Cornwall’s leaders, who secured a special devo deal under the previous Tory government, were at No 10 North last week – the hub of devolution discussions – hammering out an enhanced set of powers matched by extra money.

Yet there is concern that while these areas might come on board before next year, many others will be left out.

Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit, a thinktank, said: “A rewired state needs every tier of government to play its part, and it needs every tier of government to be financially resilient.”

In his view, those areas without a mayor, or without a special devo deal like Cornwall, will begin to fall behind the rest, exacerbating regional inequality.

Next month, No 10 is due to publish the much-anticipated Rewiring the State delivery plan, which Burnham has said will contain the thrust of what he wants to achieve as prime minister.

Carr-West said the holes in Healey’s speech will need to be filled in by Burnham if there is to be some clarity about the way forward. “Today’s budget statement puts more, rather than less, pressure on that document,” he said.

One of the major barriers to progress is likely to be the stalled reorganisation of local government in England, which was due to convert county and district councils into a web of unitary authorities. Angela Rayner, the secretary of state for housing, local government and communities, suspended the plan in September.

Unitary authorities will carry out all the roles previously divided between counties and districts, from providing social services and education to overseeing parking and local business licences.

Several county councils have used judicial reviews to challenge the plans, forcing Rayner to rethink.

Kent is an example of an authority that is a long way from having an MSA, after the Reform UK-run county council objected to a government plan for a split into four unitaries. It has gone to court saying Kent should remain as a single entity, much like Cornwall.

Vince Maple, head of Medway council in Kent, accepts the dispute is a barrier to a deal at the moment, but says it was clear from Healey’s speech that local government reorganisation (LGR) will go ahead in some form and devo deals will follow.

“Government has made itself clear that LGR is going ahead. Most people accept it will happen,” he said.

Maple also heads the Key Cities Group of second-tier urban areas, which includes Gloucester, Sunderland and Salford. He said the expansion of MSAs to include a further 10 areas meant the government was getting closer to its “every postcode” target.

“Our members will be part of the conversation now in a way that they weren’t 24 hours ago,” he said.

There is also scepticism that the economic growth Burnham hopes to achieve from devolution may be slow to materialise.

In a judgment on the budget, the consultancy Oxford Economics , said: “A combination of limited detail, unaddressed challenges, and the length of time for any upside to show means that the devolution announcements will not lead us to revising our regional forecasts.”

Burnham will hope that rearranging the structure of local government will be enough at the next election to convince voters that change is beneficial, even if he cannot show a boost to economic growth.

OBR cautions about Middle East war dragging down growth and triggering a fresh cost of living crisis

Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

Budget 2026 live – latest updates

British households face a “grim picture” for living standards as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, the government’s independent forecaster has said.

As John Healey announced his first budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) issued its report showing a sharp downgrade for growth in 2027, household disposable incomes and the public finances, despite the measures taken by the chancellor .

Although Healey sought to cushion the blow through “breathing space” policies to help with soaring energy costs, the watchdog said household disposable incomes after taking account of inflation would fall by 0.6% next year. The downgrade - compared with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes that the OBR was forecasting in March – was driven mainly by higher energy costs.

While forecasting a modest recovery from next year, the OBR warned that families were facing among the weakest decades for growth in real household disposable income on records dating back to the 1960s.

Setting the stage for a tough election run-up for Labour, the watchdog said disposable incomes in 2029, after taking account of inflation, were on track to be only 1% higher than in 2019 – before the onset of the Covid pandemic.

“It’s a pretty grim picture”, David Miles of the OBR said.

“If you go back to just before Covid, and take that as your base, where we are right now - seven years later, is virtually no growth in per person real household disposable income,” he said.

“That’s pretty unusual in the history of the UK.”

As the impact from Donald Trump’s war hits British households, businesses and the government finances, Healey said the exchequer was spending £14bn more on debt interest as the financial market fallout from the conflict pushes up borrowing costs for countries worldwide.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, the chancellor said he would allow a hit to his buffer against the government’s fiscal rules – while also announcing a temporary rise in tax on banks to fund his package of energy support.

He left £15bn of headroom against the main fiscal rule , which requires day-to-day spending to be matched by tax receipts in three years’ time – down from £23.6bn left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, in the spring.

As a consequence, the OBR said borrowing was poised to fall to about 2% of GDP in the medium term but at a slower near-term pace than previous plans.

after newsletter promotion

As the energy price shock rippling out from the Middle East hits households and businesses, the OBR said consumers would face inflation of 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.

Healey made helping families with the cost of living a core focus of his first budget, including £100 in blanket payments for 20 million households at a cost to the exchequer of £2.6bn and a plan to abolish standing charges on gas bills .

However, with the fallout from the war steadily mounting, the OBR warned that Britain’s resilience to the conflict that had been recorded so far this year would begin to fizzle out.

While it upgrades its growth forecast for this year from 1.1% to 1.2% after an unexpectedly resilient performance fuelled by AI investment, it slashed its estimate for next year from 1.5% to 1%.

Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war, after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.

Although saying he would never be complacent, Healey said there were “signs of resilience” in the economy as he highlighted that the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund had issued growth upgrades for the UK within recent months.

“There are real challenges ahead but Britain has beaten the forecasts this year, and with the action I am taking today I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said.

However, the economy is coming under mounting pressure from the energy price shock triggered by the war. Since the start of the US-Israeli led invasion of Iran at the end of February, which has throttled energy flows in the region, oil prices have risen from about $70 a barrel to more than $115, while gas prices have almost tripled.

With a tentative pause in the fighting while Trump prepares for crunch midterm elections, the OBR said the outlook for the economy, households and the UK public finances remained highly uncertain.

Suggesting there were “significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability”, it said that if energy prices were to rise to a higher and more sustained peak, government borrowing could be £17bn above the central forecast next year. However, a lower energy price path could reduce borrowing by £12bn.

Would the Chancellor improve credibility with voters by reminding us of the costs of COVID and Ukraine?

RichienotsoRich asks : Question for Hilary/Heather. Would the Chancellor, and all politicians for that matter, improve their credibility with voters by reminding us of the one off costs that the country endured due to COVID and Ukraine? Estimates for COVID range up to £410bn. The Energy Cap in 2022 another maybe £150bn. That translates into perhaps half a Second World War. Obviously Brexit costs can be estimated too but the debate falls into tribalism. The others are essential context surely?

double quotation mark Heather says: Yes, I think every chancellor should mention this repeatedly, and I would chuck in the global financial crisis too, as one of the three shocks (four if you include this latest war) that have contributed to the debt-to-GDP ratio being where it is today. Labour do talk about the costs of the Ukraine crisis but it tends to be bundled up into a “Liz Truss crashed the economy” argument. It was welcome I thought that John Healey was clear in his budget speech about the importance of global events - ie Donald Trump’s Middle East conflict - in driving the current crisis. There are some great historic charts of debt here , if you’re interested.

How does the budget affect the devolved nations?

CraftyInnit asks : Plaid Cymru claimed yesterday that (references to the Welsh budget suggest) that the settlement for Wales won’t meet the increases due to inflation. Real-time cuts. The Guardian’s article about devolution skimmed over the devolved nations, dismissively.

Could you comment on how the budget affects the settlements with the devolved nations? It is very difficult to find any information on this (or anything to do with the devolved nations) here.

double quotation mark Heather says: You’re right that the devolution proposals contained in yesterday’s budget were about how the Westminster government allocates funding to local authorities in England. Separately, Andy Burnham is in discussions with Scotland about a new devolution deal, and he said at prime minister’s questions before the budget that he would be extending a similar offer to Wales, on Friday. Aside from that, the funding behind decisions made at the budget - the £100 cost of living payment for example - will be filtered down to Scotland and Wales as ever, with the devolved governments left to decide how to allocate the money. I haven’t looked at the Welsh settlement in detail but rising inflation is definitely putting pressure on spending everywhere.

What does the increase in tax free allowance for pensioners really mean?

nannyd66 asks : Please can you explain what the increase in tax free allowance for pensioners will mean. I get 33 quid a month from a private pension, will I be better off or worse off!

double quotation mark Hilary says: I’ll have a go! The new allowance is designed to make sure that people who are relying on the new state pension do not face a tax bill when, thanks to the triple lock, it exceeds the personal tax allowance next year. Before the budget there were worries that introducing a new allowance just for those relying wholly on the pension would penalise people who get just a small amount on top from elsewhere. Instead, the chancellor announced a new allowance for all pensioners. Anyone with a total income below £13,037 will not pay income tax, while those with an income between £13,037 and £13,319 will receive some of the allowance and pay less income tax as a result. However, assuming your £33 a month is on top of the new state pension your income takes you above £13,319 so you won’t benefit. You will pay tax on everything above the regular personal allowance of £12,570. You won’t be worse off than if the allowance didn’t exist, but you will pay some of your state pension back in tax.

Why isn't the payment going direct to energy suppliers?

manicmid asks: Why isn’t the £100 payment being paid direct to energy suppliers like the previous £300 energy support?

I guess it’s because there is the council tax band qualifying criteria this time but it does mean the £100 could be spent on anything else rather than energy bills?

double quotation mark Heather says: Yes, according to John Healey the £100 is being paid straight into consumers’ bank accounts, so presumably you can spend it on whatever you like - much like Winter Fuel Allowance, which could equally be spent on a night out in the pub. I’m not sure why they’re doing it this way: but my hunch is they think it will be more likely to be noticed, and credited to the government, than a discount on a bill that will still be rising.

What is happening regarding green energy for homeowners?

Flipchart45 asks : There was a lot of pre-budget speculation about reducing or abolishing grants for heat-pumps. I haven’t seen any detail of this in the budget information I’ve read. Could anyone enlighten me on what is happening regarding green energy for homeowners?

double quotation mark Hilary says: You’re right, and the good news for homeowners planning green upgrades was that things were not as bad as anticipated. Funding for the boiler upgrade scheme was supposed to go up to £600m, but is being kept at £400m. Grants remain the same though, so you can still apply for £7,500 towards a heat pump (or £9,000 if you’re not on mains gas). A new loan scheme was also announced , offering households low or no-interest borrowing to pay for improvements such as heat pumps, batteries and solar panels. The loan and the grant can be combined.

Why no reform of Council Tax?

jonny2bad asks : Is there any reason, technical or otherwise, why reform of Council Tax is completely off the table? It seems that it would be a sure fire win if such an announcement was made as it demonstrates a desire for progressive changes which directly reduce inequality. Of course there would be costs involved but I am baffled why this topic does not even register with the government’s business.

double quotation mark Heather says: I don’t think there’s any technical reason, it’s all about the politics. It would be likely to mean significantly higher bills for people in more valuable properties - no doubt leading to a noisy backlash, including highlighting the cases of people with high-value homes but smaller incomes (pensioners for example). Another objection used to be the difficulties of doing a revaluation, but online data would surely make that much easier today. So it’s all about having the political courage to make the argument. It would help tackle inequality, as you rightly say; but it would also have losers, of course.

How does the extra 2% tax on savings interest affect the starting rate for savings?

andya2015 asks: How does the extra 2% tax on savings interest affect the starting rate for savings which allows you to earn up to £5,000 in interest income tax-free assuming your other taxable income (like wages or pension) is low (below £17,570)?

I assume you don’t pay the extra 2% if the starting rate for savings covers all of your interest income?

Also, I assume the extra 2% is only levied on interest income in excess of your personal savings allowance of either £500 or £1000?

double quotation mark Hilary says: The new savings tax rate will only be applied to interest you are earning after you’ve used up all the allowances you are eligible for - that includes the £20,000 you can put in an Isa each tax year, and your personal savings allowance. The personal savings allowance is £1,000 a year for basic rate taxpayers, and £500 for higher-rate payers, and £0 for additional rate payers - that’s how much interest you can earn without paying tax. The starting rate, as you mention, gives you an extra £5,000 allowance if you are on a low income Again, this will be applied before you are charged any tax. If you combine the Isa with your personal savings allowance, as a basic-rate tax payer you can save about £45,000 at an interest rate of 4% without facing the new charge.

What is going to stop landlord just transferring their tax increase onto tenants?

FelonMarmer asks : What is going to stop landlords just transferring their tax increase onto tenants, while complaining about how hard done by they are?

double quotation mark Heather says : Unfortunately, there’s nothing to stop landlords passing their higher tax bills onto their tenants, aside from what the local rental market will bear. Indeed, the Office for Budget Responsibility did suggest one result of this and other recent policies (the 2p rise this year followed another 2p last year) could be “a steady rise in rents,” as some landlords whack up rents and others leave the market altogether. I think John Healey’s answer would probably be a fairness one - that income made through renting out property should be taxed more heavily than that earned through work.

Would Labour have been elected if they campaigned on higher income taxes?

manicmid asks: This budget was always going to consist of multiple instances of tinkering around the edges and deferring big unpopular choices.

Labour sealed that position by sticking to their previous manifesto that removed rises on the biggest revenue raisers such as income tax.

However, would Labour have been elected if they campaigned on higher income taxes?

double quotation mark Heather says: That’s a really good question: Labour strategists are adamant that they wouldn’t. I can’t help thinking that voters were so convinced the public services were in a dire state, they could have accepted the argument that taxes needed to rise. Certainly, the Tories didn’t seem to get much electoral credit for Jeremy Hunt’s desperate cuts to national insurance contributions in his last couple of budgets. But we’ll never know. Another question is whether Labour should have bust the manifesto promises - either when they first got in, on the basis the public finances were worse than they thought; or at some point in the last year, given the impact of the Iran war (which has added £14bn to the government’s interest costs this year alone).

Isn’t the £100 handout just giving tax payers money to the energy companies but using customers as a conduit?

Takemetoyourleader asks: I am as always willing to admit my ignorance regarding economics, but isn’t the £100 handout rather like giving tax payers money to the energy companies but using customers as a conduit? It doesn’t solve the problem. It just buys ten days’ energy.

double quotation mark Heather says: Well John Healey’s not going to tell you how to spend your £100, so I suppose you could blow it on the horses instead - but yes, we can’t really get away from the fact that higher energy prices make the UK, an energy importer, poorer – hence the government’s rhetoric of, we can’t offset this completely but we’ll try and help you out a bit. He could of course have decided to go a little, or a lot, further: taxing banks more heavily for example to fund a more generous package. He has also announced some longer-term changes aimed at bringing down energy costs to insulate us better from future shocks; but these look unlikely to bear fruit for a long time.

Why has the Chancellor left the very wealthiest untouched?

JakeAtkinson asks : Why has the Chancellor left the very wealthiest untouched? Take the increase in the bank surcharge - why is it only temporary? It also leaves billions on the table compared to proposals for a windfall tax on the banks’ domestic UK retail income; meanwhile they continue to make excessive profits - news today is that Lloyds pre-tax profits have almost doubled.

Also Capital Gains Tax wasn’t reform to tax income from wealth equally as income from work, with an investment allowance to account for inflation and reforms to the base, this equalisation could raise £19 billion a year too.

Lots left on the table by not taxing wealth.

double quotation mark Heather says : There’s certainly an argument that more could be raised by a proportional tax on wealth - though the most straightforward way squeeze more from the super rich is probably, as you say, an overhaul of capital gains tax. That would have to include closing various loopholes, so raising the rate didn’t result in massive avoidance; but plenty of experts argue that it’s feasible to do that - including at the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) and CenTax, at Warwick University. I think Labour have repeatedly been scared off this, because they don’t want to send out the wrong vibes to global investors - but I agree with you it’s a shame they haven’t just cracked on with it. When it comes to the bank tax, I imagine the Treasury was lobbied hard by the sector, and warned that they would pass on the costs to customers in higher interest rates - but they could have been bolder, and perhaps made the change longer-lasting too.

Will customers not on mains gas benefit from the standing charge removal?

DrJWCC asks: For those of us who live out in the wilds, who are not on mains gas (as in, LPG tanks) will we benefit from standing charge removal? I’m assuming not.

double quotation mark Hilary says : I’m afraid the standing charge removal will not help you, but some of the other measures will hopefully reduce your overall energy bills. The extension of the VAT cut on energy will be for everyone, so that’s about £50 off your annual costs. If you live in council tax bands A-D you will get the £100 payment in January. And there are some measures targeted at people who are not on mains gas. Tariffs on kerosene are being scrapped for two years, which should reduce costs for those who rely on heating oil, and the boiler upgrade scheme was left untouched. The scheme offers £9,000 to homeowners in England and Wales who want to install a heatpump.

Why the opposition to lifting the tax threshold?

Guardiangirl66 asks : Why are governments so stubbornly opposed to lifting the basic tax threshold? They adjust them to fit some people affected by fiscal drag but not others, which can’t be cheap to implement and it isn’t fair either.

Tax thresholds need to be universally applied in each band, and be simple and crystal clear. Some tapering is overdue to avoid cliff edges and high marginal tax rates but it must be for everyone.

double quotation mark Heather says : If you mean the basic rate threshold, it did rise repeatedly from 2010-2020, starting under the Conservative/LibDem coalition, to 44% of average earnings - but yes it’s been frozen for quite a while since, so it kicks in at about 34% of average earnings now. I think the Labour objection to raising it further would be that it’s not a very progressive way of making a tax cut, because it’s set so high already (£12,570) that the lowest earners already don’t pay tax and so wouldn’t benefit from further rises. Completely agree re complicated tweaks to the system, though - the simpler and clearer it is, the better.

Is there anything in this budget for young working people?

southlondon1 asks: Is there anything in this budget for young working people? I’m 27, renting a 1 bed with my partner in London, and barely earn enough money to save £50 a month, let alone save for a house. I feel like yet again the government are leaving out people like me who are nowhere near buying a house, have no children (and couldn’t afford it anyway) and our rent costs half our salary. £100 doesn’t really provide any breathing space.

double quotation mark Hilary says: The main measure for young renters was the Your First Home scheme, which will mean you can think about buying a property when you have a deposit of 2.5%, but in London if you can only save £50 a month that is likely to feel a long way off. Unfortunately there was not much else that’s immediately going to help you. The thresholds for student loan repayments and income tax remain the same, so if you get a pay rise you will see your take home pay go up by less than had these risen in line with inflation. The £100 energy payment comes alongside the removal of VAT on your electricity bills, and the planned removal of the standing charge on gas, so that’s a bit more money you will keep. However, with energy prices looking set to rise in January it’s likely you will still see your bills rise.

Is this budget really just a sticking plaster?

CordTrousers asks : Diesel is still at £1.99 a litre at our local station. That means inflation is going to remain elevated, as it feeds through to more everyday commodities there is going to be building pressure for wage increases ... Which will fuel inflation some more. After the midterms, it looks likely Trump will renew his attacks on Iran. A light touch budget like this then, feels a temporary measure. Really there’s nothing the UK can do but tighten its belt when we have such a constraint on fuel supply, is there?

double quotation mark Heather says: You’re absolutely right that as an energy-importing country, it’s just a fact that a crisis like the one we’re going through makes us poorer. So I think John Healey’s message that the government can’t completely insulate consumers, but want to do a bit to help, is probably the right one. But whether he’s done enough remains to be seen - inflation is set to rise further, as you say, and the Bank of England is likely to raise interest rates next week, so that £100 cost of living payment might not look so generous by the New Year. Obviously the government is hoping the Iran conflict will subside, which might allow oil prices to fall, and the economy to bounce back (GDP growth was actually pretty strong in the first half of this year). Time will tell.

Hilary and Heather are live

Hilary and Heather are online now answering your 2026 budget questions

Welcome to the conversation

Yesterday Chancellor John Healey gave his maiden budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, announcing measures to cut energy bills funded by a windfall tax on banks. He characterised his plan as “ a budget built on fiscal discipline ” fit to face “global economic storms” that are driving up up energy prices.

Does Healey’s budget represent a break with the past, or is the lower-than-expected tax on banks just another example of tinkering around the edges by another Chancellor fenced in by self-imposed fiscal rules?

Hilary Osborne , the Guardian’s money and consumer editor will be joining economics editor Heather Stewart from 3pm (GMT) today to answer your questions on the outlook for our economy.

Sign up or sign in to join the discussion. Post your questions in the comments below.

Payments to 20m homes part of package to cut energy bills and ease cost of living crisis, paid for by bank windfall tax

‘A pretty grim picture’: outlook for UK living standards slashed despite Healey’s budget

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

John Healey promised to steer Britain through “global economic storms” as he announced an energy giveaway of £100 to 80% of households in England, funded by a smaller than expected windfall tax on banks.

In his first budget, the chancellor said 20 million households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 payment – a measure he said would cost £2.6bn.

That includes equivalent funding for Scotland and Wales, whose governments can decide whether to replicate the measure. The policy will help a large number of middle earners, reaching houses worth up to about £600,000 in London.

“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said, announcing the payment.

The relief on bills comes at a cost to big banks via the banking surcharge rise, and to savers and landlords, who were hit with an unexpected tax rise.

Healey said his budget would shape Britain’s future on defence, energy, welfare and entrepreneurship. “This Labour government has set a course for fresh hope, good growth and support for those who need it.”

The chancellor also extended the VAT cut on electricity bills until next July, and as widely expected, cancelled fuel duty rises pencilled in by Rachel Reeves.

Healey said this would help businesses as well as consumers. “For millions of people, the cost of living and the cost of doing business are the same. The home is the office. The van is the family car,” he said.

He blamed the war in the Middle East for the deterioration in the economic outlook since Reeves’s spring statement, but insisted he would keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track.

“Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” he said, describing his statement as “a budget built on fiscal discipline, which matches immediate action today with clear direction for the future”.

He said higher inflation as a result of the Iran war was expected to cost the government £14bn more in interest costs and the Office for Budget Responsibility had downgraded its growth forecast to 1% for next year, from the 1.6% it expected in the spring.

Healey nevertheless promised to meet Labour’s first fiscal rule, on balancing current spending with tax receipts by 2029-30, but with diminished headroom of £15bn – against the £24bn that Reeves set aside in March. He said the cushion would be rebuilt to £22bn by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can.”

The chancellor said the energy package would be funded by a windfall tax on Britain’s banks and the unexpected two percentage-point income tax rise for landlords and savers.

after newsletter promotion

He is doubling the additional levy the banks pay on their profits to 6% from the current 3% for 15 months from January. That fell short of the rise to 8% that many industry figures had expected.

Healey lavished praise on the sector as he announced the measure. “I want to say directly to our banks: I celebrate and I am grateful for the role that you play,” he said. Bank share prices rose after the announcement, with NatWest and Standard Chartered up by more than 4%.

Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.

There was a package of policies that Healey said would tackle the “moral mission” of homelessness.

There will be no easing of fiscal drag, however, despite Andy Burnham previously expressing concern at the rate at which households were being pulled into higher rates of income tax.

Forecasts show that the freeze on tax thresholds will drag an extra 6.7m people into paying income tax and push 5.4m more into the higher rate band by 2031–32. The minimum wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 an hour, an increase of £910 to the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker.

Pensions will also rise thanks to the triple lock, but with new tax relief to keep pensioners from paying income tax as the state pension rises above the personal allowance for the first time. About 500,000 pensioners are to benefit.

Healey also announced sweeping new powers for regions, pledging all mayors would be given a share of income tax revenue from 2028. He said he intended that local and regional government would retain 100% of business rates income before the end of the decade.

He said the devolution package would be “new powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics”.
